The Old Man Who Lost His Horse: Does Withholding Judgment Mean Never Judging?
A family lived near the frontier. One day, a horse suddenly ran off across the border.
The neighbors came to offer their sympathy.
But the old man of the household said:
How do you know this will not turn out to be a good thing?
A few months later, the horse returned, bringing a fine horse with it. The neighbors came to congratulate the family.
The old man said:
How do you know this will not turn out to be a bad thing?
Now the family had a fine horse, and the young man enjoyed riding it. Later, he fell off and broke his leg. Once again, the neighbors came to offer their sympathy.
The old man said, as before:
How do you know this will not turn out to be a good thing?

A year later, war broke out along the frontier. Many able-bodied young men were called up to fight, and casualties were heavy. Because of his injured leg, this young man did not go to war, and father and son both survived.
The story is often compressed into a single saying:
Bad things can turn into good things, and good things into bad.
That is certainly part of the story.
But if we take it to mean “There is no need to feel sad about anything bad, because it might benefit you later,” it quickly becomes a cruel form of comfort.
When the horse ran away, the loss was real.
When the leg broke, the pain and restricted movement were real, too.
Surviving later did not mean the fracture had never happened.
What, then, was the old man refusing when he repeatedly declined to say “This is misfortune” or “This is good fortune”?
He was not denying the facts before him.
He was refusing this:
**To settle an event's entire meaning within a life the moment it happens.**
After the horse ran away, the family did indeed have one horse fewer.
The neighbors who offered sympathy were not entirely mistaken.
If the horse provided transport, labor, or wealth, its departure would cause real difficulties. The family could search for it, adjust their lives, and feel sorry for the loss.
The old man did not say:
This is no loss.
He said:
How do you know it will not be the beginning of something else?
There is a considerable difference.
“This is no loss” denies the present.
“It may have other consequences yet” limits the scope of a present judgment.
We readily sort something that has just happened into one of two categories:
Success or failure.
Good luck or bad luck.
Worthwhile or not worthwhile.
Such judgments are useful. They help us decide whether to put things right, whether to stop, and what to do next.
The problem is that after making a present judgment, we often take one step further:
Because this attempt failed, the whole path was wrong.
Because I gained something this time, the future is secure.
Because it hurts now, this experience can only be a loss.
Because it feels right now, no later consequence will call for a second look.
Each time the old man asks “How do you know?”, he is not asking us never to judge.
He is simply taking back that extra step.
When the horse returned with a fine companion, the neighbors came to congratulate the family.
There was nothing wrong with that, either.
What the family had lost was back, along with a new resource. Feeling happy about the gain before them was a normal response to reality.
Nor did the old man say:
This is not a good thing.
His reminder was this:
Acquiring something also changes what can happen next.
New abilities bring new actions.
New wealth brings new choices.
New opportunities can also lead us into risks we would otherwise never have encountered.
This does not mean that the more we gain, the more danger we face. Nor does it mean we must imagine the worst whenever something good happens, to keep ourselves from being happy.
If every joy must immediately be canceled out by a future risk, caution becomes another way of being unable to live.
The distinction that matters is this:
We can be happy about a present gain without declaring, in our happiness, that it will bring only good forever after.
Joy does not need a permanent guarantee to count as joy.
Nor must caution abolish joy to count as caution.
After the young man is injured, the story reaches its most easily misread moment.
War comes later, and his injury spares him from fighting and saves his life.
People may therefore look back and say:
How lucky that he broke his leg.
In light of the outcome, the remark is understandable. Without that injury, he might have died in the war.
But the claim still needs limits.
The injury was harm when it happened.

It caused pain, restrictions, and lasting effects. The later war changed the place of that injury within his life as a whole. It did not turn the injury itself into something one ought deliberately to inflict.
If someone knew war was coming, deliberately broke a young man's leg, and then said “This is to save you,” that would be an entirely different act.
The father and son did not choose the fracture, nor did they have certain knowledge of the war to come.
The fact that an accidental injury later prevented a greater harm does not directly imply:
So causing the original injury was right.
This distinction matters enormously.
Good consequences may change how we understand an event, without necessarily justifying, in retrospect, every action that brought it about.
Otherwise, any later benefit would allow earlier harm, negligence, and injustice to be renamed a necessary process.
Real life is not that tidy.
Equally, the story does not prove:
Every bad thing will turn out well in the end.
The horse might never return.
The young man might break his leg in a year without a war.
Someone spared from fighting might suffer losses for other reasons.

The Huainanzi says that misfortune and good fortune transform into one another in ways difficult to exhaust or measure. This is an openness of consequences, not a cosmic guarantee that every account will be fairly settled.
“Things may get better later” cannot be treated as a promise.
It cannot demand immediate gratitude from someone who is suffering, or release onlookers from the responsibility to help.

When someone loses a job, a relationship breaks down, or a plan fails, saying “Perhaps this is a good thing” is sometimes less an act of wisdom than an attempt to stop their pain from inconveniencing us.
Once we name the loss a future gift, we no longer have to face what it is doing now.
The old man's answer is not that kind of consolation.
At least in the language of the story, he does not declare:
This will certainly be good fortune.
He simply refuses to let others declare too quickly:
This can only be misfortune.
Holding off on a final judgment does not mean doing nothing.
We cannot wait for every consequence to unfold before we act.
When the horse runs away, we must decide whether to search, given the conditions at hand.
When the young man is injured, the injury and his care need attention.
When war comes, the immediate danger must be faced.
We always live with incomplete information.
Wisdom cannot therefore consist merely of saying, over and over:
We do not know yet. Let us wait.
If waiting allows avoidable harm to grow, refusing to judge becomes a decision in its own right.
What we need to distinguish are two kinds of judgment:
A limited judgment made for the sake of acting now.
And a final verdict on what an event means within an entire life.
The first often cannot wait.
The second often comes too soon.
We can say:
This loss needs to be dealt with.
This outcome makes me happy.
This decision appears, for now, to have failed.
This experience harmed me.
While still leaving room for this:
I do not yet know what it may connect with later, or whether today's judgment encompasses all its meaning.
This is not wavering.
It is asking a judgment to answer only for what it actually knows.
There is another easily missed detail in the fable.
Whenever events change, the neighbors' judgments change with them.
The horse leaves, and they offer comfort.
The horse returns, and they offer congratulations.
The young man is injured, and they offer comfort again.
They are not stupid. Each time, they simply treat the most conspicuous present result as though the whole event were finished.
The old man knows no more of the future than they do.
When the horse first goes missing, he does not know it will return.
When the fine horse arrives, he does not know the young man will fall.
When the leg breaks, he does not necessarily know that war will come a year later.
What he has is not prophecy.
It is an awareness of what he does not know.
That is what distinguishes his “How do you know?” from a performance of profundity.
He does not reject everyone's judgment because he possesses a hidden answer. He refuses to let the current answer pass for the whole answer precisely because he possesses no hidden answer.
Still, this attitude has dangers of its own.
Someone can use “Who knows what will bring good fortune or bad?” to avoid admitting a mistake.
A plan fails, and they say the future may yet prove them right.
They hurt someone, and say it may help that person grow.
They refuse to change for years, and say present consequences are not the final outcome.
If every piece of contrary evidence can be postponed into the future, “not rushing to judge” becomes a way of never accepting reality.
Leaving the future open does not erase the past and present.
Until new consequences appear, the consequences already here still have to be acknowledged.
If a decision repeatedly causes foreseeable harm, we cannot keep using good fortune that has not happened to cancel misfortune that has.
If others suffer losses because of our actions, we cannot say:
How do you know this will not be good for you someday?
The openness of the future cannot be an escape route from responsibility.
It limits our tendency to inflate a partial result into a complete meaning. It does not limit our responsibility for the consequences we have already caused.
Perhaps the most defensible wisdom of the old man who lost his horse is not optimism.
It is not even a midpoint between optimism and pessimism.
It is a form of restraint about time:
Take seriously what has happened before you.
Do not speak the last word on what the present has not yet revealed.
We can grieve a loss without declaring that our whole life has been defined by it.
We can rejoice in a gain without assuming that every future risk has disappeared.
We can acknowledge the harm an event caused while allowing later connections to change our understanding of its place in the whole.
Past facts do not vanish because of later outcomes.
But an event's meaning need not be closed on the day it happens, either.
At the end of the story, the young man's injured leg spares him from war, and father and son survive.
It is a powerful ending, which helps explain why the story has endured.
But the lesson we carry into everyday judgment should not be:
Bad things always turn into good things.
It should be:
**We must act without knowing every consequence, but we need not present limited knowledge as a final conclusion.**
What needs repair still needs repair.
What gives us cause for happiness can still make us happy.
Responsibility that must be faced cannot be handed over to the future.
But when we are about to judge a whole life by one gain or loss, define a person by one outcome, or declare from today's pain that no possibilities remain, we can pause.
And ask:
Is what I know now one part of this event, or enough to stand for the whole?
Not rushing to settle the account does not mean never judging.
It means making a present judgment when action is needed, and refusing, when we cannot know the whole, to disguise that judgment as fate.

*Textual basis: the passage beginning “Among those living near the frontier was a man skilled in the arts” in the Huainanzi, “Lessons of the Human World,” and its surrounding discussion. The original introduces the story with “The transformations through which misfortune and good fortune give rise to one another are hard to discern,” and concludes, “Good fortune becomes misfortune, and misfortune good fortune; their transformations cannot be exhausted, their depths cannot be measured.” This essay retains that context of inexhaustible change while distinguishing present gains and losses, subsequent consequences, responsibility for actions, and a final reckoning of a life's meaning.*
